claim: Resistance makes muscles work against force.
evidence_excerpt: causes the body’s muscles to work or hold against an applied force or weight.
limitations: General definition; not an account of the fictional recording.

claim: Repeated strength training and recovery can improve strength.
evidence_excerpt: muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activities overload muscles and bones, making them stronger. | To give your muscles time to recover, rest one full day
limitations: Combines adaptation and recovery guidance; no guaranteed individual gain or timeline.

claim: A manageable challenge can increase gradually as capacity improves.
evidence_excerpt: Small, progressive changes in overload help the body adapt to the additional stresses while minimizing the risk of injury.
limitations: Progression does not eliminate injury risk; no dose prescribed.

claim: The same weight can require different relative effort across people or training stages.
evidence_excerpt: Intensity, or how much weight or force is used relative to how much a person is able to lift; | you'll likely be able to lift weight more easily
limitations: Relative effort paraphrase; weights alone cannot establish subjective effort.

claim: Pain is not the objective; the fictional coach stops painful exercise.
evidence_excerpt: If a strength training exercise causes pain, stop the exercise.
limitations: Normative safety guidance; source does not authenticate the fictional coach or imply all discomfort is injury.

claim: One exhausting session is not an instant fitness upgrade.
evidence_excerpt: progress to higher levels of physical activity by continued overload and adaptation. | improvement in your strength and physical function over time.
limitations: Addresses durable training improvement; does not deny acute effects from a single session.

claim: Brisk walking increases heart and breathing demands.
evidence_excerpt: Brisk walking, running, bicycling, jumping rope, and swimming are all examples. Aerobic activity causes a person’s heart to beat faster, and they will breathe harder than normal.
limitations: General aerobic physiology; fictional footage is illustrative.

claim: Regular aerobic training can improve fitness over time, including stationary exercise.
evidence_excerpt: aerobic physical activity places a stress on the cardiorespiratory system and muscles | This increase in demand increases the efficiency and capacity
limitations: Adaptation depends on activity and individual capacity; geographic travel is not a physiological requirement.

claim: Appropriate starting effort and plans depend on individual capacity.
evidence_excerpt: The initial amount of activity should be at a light or moderate intensity, for short periods of time | work with a trainer or other fitness specialist to learn correct form
limitations: The different recovered plans are fiction; the general individual-capacity principle is supported.

claim: Exercise can support everyday function; outcomes and abilities vary.
evidence_excerpt: Strength training can improve physical function | It may improve your ability to do everyday activities
limitations: No guarantee of reaching a particular trail, curing disease, or reversing every limitation.

claim: A gym is optional: strength training at home and outdoor physical activity are possible.
evidence_excerpt: You can do strength training at home or in the gym. | running, bicycling, jumping rope, and swimming
limitations: Suitable activities depend on individual needs; access to a gym is not required for all activity.

claim: Leaving the gym does not establish cessation of activity or permanent fitness; Mara continues walks and home exercise.
evidence_excerpt: continued overload and adaptation | If you stick with it, you can continue to increase your strength
limitations: Scientific consistency check only. Later journal entries are fictional evidence of continuing activity, not sourced clinical outcomes.
